prompt: In `labels := Map(ages, strconv.Itoa)`, where does the compiler find the type for `U`?
hint: `Map` is declared `func Map[T, U any](xs []T, f func(T) U) []U`.

choices.text: In `labels`, the variable the result goes into
choices.why: Inference never looks outside the call; `labels` gets its type from the result, not the other way round.

choices.text: In the type of `strconv.Itoa`, `func(int) string`
choices.why: Right. It matches `func(T) U` with `T` as `int` and `U` as `string`.

choices.text: Nowhere, so `U` becomes `any`
choices.why: A type parameter that cannot be inferred is an error, never a silent `any`; and `%T` printed `[]string`.

choices.text: In the import of `strconv`, which declares string types
choices.why: An import says which package a name comes from; the type comes from the function's signature.

prompt: What does the compiler do with `var labels []string = Make(2)`, where `func Make[T any](n int) []T`?
hint: Where does `T` appear in `Make`'s parameters?

choices.text: Compiles, with `T` read from the type of `labels`
choices.why: That is the common belief the section names; line 19 of `~/generic2-infer` refutes it.

choices.text: Compiles, and `Make` returns an empty `[]string`
choices.why: It never gets as far as running: `T` has no value, so there is no `Make` to call.

choices.text: Refuses it: `cannot infer T`
choices.why: Right. `T` is only in the result, and inference reads the arguments; write `Make[string](2)`.

choices.text: Compiles with `T` as `any`, then fails to assign `[]any` to `labels`
choices.why: There is no default to `any`; the first and only error is `cannot infer T`.

prompt: Filling in a type parameter, as `Make[string](2)` does by naming `string` at the call, is called explicit ___.
hint: The section bolds the word.

prompt: Why was `Biggest(count, price)` refused, with `count` an `int` and `price` a `float64`?
hint: `Biggest(3, 2.5)` compiled two lines earlier.

choices.text: `Biggest` cannot compare two `float64` values
choices.why: It compared `3` and `2.5` as `float64` and printed `3 float64`.

choices.text: `count` fixed `T` as `int`, and `price` is another type
choices.why: Right: `type float64 of price does not match inferred type int for T`. One `T` per call, and Go converts nothing for you.

choices.text: Typed variables cannot be passed to a generic function, only constants
choices.why: `Biggest(float64(count), price)` passed two typed values and ran.

choices.text: The compiler picked `float64` for both, then refused `count`
choices.why: That choice is only possible for untyped constants; here the first argument already had a type, `int`.

prompt: With `Map` and `Make` as declared in `~/generic2`, which of these lines compile? Choose every one that does.
hint: Is there an argument to read each type parameter from, or is it written?

choices.text: `toText := Map[int, string]`
choices.why: Yes: every type filled in, so it is an ordinary function value.

choices.text: `Map[int](ages, strconv.Itoa)`
choices.why: Yes: `T` is written and `U` is still read off `strconv.Itoa`.

choices.text: `names := Make(2)`
choices.why: No: `cannot infer T`, since `T` appears only in the result.

choices.text: `toText := Map`
choices.why: No: `cannot use generic function Map without instantiation`.

prompt: `func Map[T, U any](xs []T, f func(T) U) []U` is called as `Map[int](ages, strconv.Itoa)`. How many of its type parameters did the compiler infer?
hint: The brackets at the call fill them in order, and may stop early.

prompt: What is the constraint after a type parameter's name, such as `comparable` or `int | float64`?
hint: The section says it in its first bold sentence.

choices.text: Bracket syntax with no relation to interfaces
choices.why: That is how it looks, and the section starts by correcting it: `Number` was declared with `type … interface`.

choices.text: A list of types every argument is converted into
choices.why: Nothing is converted; a `Celsius` came back as `main.Celsius`.

choices.text: An interface, read as the set of types allowed for `T`
choices.why: Right. The body is allowed whatever every type in that set supports.

choices.text: A check run on each value as the program runs
choices.why: Constraints are checked by the compiler; `Index[T any]` was refused before anything ran.

prompt: `func Index[T any](xs []T, v T) int` uses `x == v` and is refused. Where is the error reported, and why?
hint: The message was on line 7.

choices.text: Inside `Index`: some type in the set `any` describes has no `==`
choices.why: Right. The body is checked once, against the whole set, before any call.

choices.text: At the call, because strings cannot be compared with `==`
choices.why: Strings compare fine; with `comparable` the same call printed `1`.

choices.text: At the call, because the slice and the value have different types
choices.why: `[]string` and `string` make `T` a `string` consistently; the error was in the body, line 7.

choices.text: Inside `Index`, because `==` never works on a type parameter
choices.why: It works whenever the constraint allows it: `Index[T comparable]` compiled.

prompt: `Sum[T int | float64]` refuses a `[]Celsius`. What change lets `Sum` take it and still return a `Celsius`?
hint: The compiler's message suggested it.

choices.text: Convert each reading to `float64` before calling `Sum`
choices.why: That compiles, but the result is a `float64`, and the unit lesson 10 attached is gone.

choices.text: Replace the union with `any`
choices.why: Then `total += x` is refused, because `+` is not defined on every type `any` holds.

choices.text: Write the constraint as `~int | ~float64`
choices.why: Right. `~float64` holds every type whose underlying type is `float64`, and the total printed `62 main.Celsius`.

choices.text: Give `Celsius` a method named `Add`
choices.why: A union lists types, not methods; a method changes nothing about whether `Celsius` is in it.

prompt: In a constraint, `___float64` is the set of every type whose underlying type is `float64`, `Celsius` included.
hint: One character, the one the compiler said was possibly missing.

prompt: Which of these interfaces can be the type of an ordinary variable?
hint: What did `var n Number = 3` say?

choices.text: `interface{ ~int | ~float64 }`
choices.why: A union makes it constraint-only: `cannot use type Number outside a type constraint`.

choices.text: `interface{ int }`, a union of one type
choices.why: One type is still a type element, and any type element makes the interface a constraint only.

choices.text: `interface{ String() string }`
choices.why: Right. An interface of methods only works both ways, as `fmt.Stringer` did in `ShowAll` and `ShowEach`.

choices.text: `comparable`
choices.why: Its documentation says it may only be used as a type parameter constraint, not as the type of a variable.

prompt: Match each constraint to the set of types it allows.
hint: The figure draws three of them as nested boxes.

pairs.right: every type, so the body can do very little
those two, and types like `Celsius` built on them

right_distractors: only the types that have a `String` method

prompt: Why does `Pop` declare `var zero T` instead of returning a literal when the stack is empty?
hint: Which literal would be zero for a `string`, an `int` and a pointer at once?

choices.text: Go requires every `return` to name a variable
choices.why: `return top, true` returns a variable and a constant; there is no such rule.

choices.text: No literal is zero for every type, and `var` gives `T`'s own
choices.why: Right. `0`, `""` and `nil` each fit some types; `var zero T` fits all of them, and gave `""` for a `Stack[string]`.

choices.text: `nil` would work just as well for these stacks; `var` is only the convention people follow
choices.why: `nil` is not a `string` or an `int`, so `return nil, false` would be refused for those stacks.

choices.text: To reserve room in memory for the next `Push`
choices.why: `zero` is a local value that is returned and forgotten; `Push` uses `append`.

prompt: Why is `var s Stack` refused, when `var words Stack[string]` is fine?
hint: Read the first error of `~/generic2-stackbad`.

choices.text: A generic type's zero value cannot be used, so it needs `&Stack{}`
choices.why: `var words Stack[string]` used the zero value and pushed onto it; `&Stack{}` is refused for the same reason as `var s Stack`.

choices.text: `Stack` is not a type until its type parameter is filled in
choices.why: Right: `cannot use generic type Stack[T any] without instantiation`. There is nothing to infer `T` from.

choices.text: `Stack` has no exported fields
choices.why: Exported names matter between packages, lesson 39; this is all one package.

choices.text: `T` defaults to `any`, and an `any` stack must be written `Stack[any]`
choices.why: There is no default; a type argument is always written for a generic type.

prompt: `Stack[T any]` needs a `Contains` that uses `==`. Which repair keeps a `Stack[[]int]` legal?
hint: Who pays for the stricter constraint in each repair?

choices.text: Declare the type as `Stack[T comparable]`
choices.why: That makes the method legal and forbids every stack of slices, `Stack[[]int]` included.

choices.text: Write the receiver as `(s *Stack[T comparable])`
choices.why: The receiver does not repeat the constraint, and writing one there is a syntax error.

choices.text: Make it a function: `func Contains[T comparable](s *Stack[T], v T) bool`
choices.why: Right. The stack stays `any`, and only `Contains` asks for more; a `Stack[[]int]` exists and cannot be passed to it.

choices.text: Compare `any(x) == any(v)` inside the method
choices.why: That compiles and moves the failure to run time: comparing two `[]int` held in `any` panics with `comparing uncomparable type []int`.

prompt: What does the compiler say to `type Mapper interface { Map[U any](f func(int) U) *Stack[U] }`?
hint: A method may have type parameters. May an interface's method?

choices.text: Nothing: it compiles when the `go` line is 1.27 or later
choices.why: The `go` line governs methods with type parameters on types; in an interface they are refused whatever it says.

choices.text: `interface method must have no type parameters`
choices.why: Right, and `undefined: U` follows, because the brackets that would have declared it were refused.

choices.text: It compiles, but only for `U` constrained by `any`
choices.why: The constraint in the capture was `any`, and it was still refused.

choices.text: It compiles if the interface itself is declared `Mapper[U any]`
choices.why: That would be a type parameter of the interface, a different thing; the method itself still may not declare one.

prompt: Order these constraints from the smallest set of types to the largest.
hint: The figure in section 03 draws three of them nested; the fourth holds everything.

prompt: `type IDs []int`. What type does `slices.Clone(ids)` return for `ids` of type `IDs`?
hint: `func Clone[S ~[]E, E any](s S) S`.

choices.text: `[]int`, because `Clone` works on plain slices
choices.why: That is what `CloneFlat` did with `[]E`; `Clone` returns `S`, the caller's own type.

choices.text: `IDs`
choices.why: Right. `S` is `IDs`, whose underlying type is `[]int`, and the result is an `S`, as `Names` came back as `main.Names`.

choices.text: `[]any`, since `E` is constrained by `any`
choices.why: `any` is the constraint on `E`, not its value; `E` is `int` here.

choices.text: Nothing: `IDs` is refused, since `S` must be exactly `[]E`
choices.why: Exactly `[]E` would be a union without `~`; the `~` is there to admit types like `IDs`.

prompt: `*Stack[int]` has `Map[U any](f func(int) U) *Stack[U]`. Does it satisfy `interface { Map(f func(int) string) *Stack[string] }`?
hint: Read the `have` and `want` lines.

choices.text: Yes, with `U` inferred as `string` from the interface
choices.why: Inference reads a call's arguments; an interface is not a call, and the compiler printed `wrong type for method Map`.

choices.text: Yes, as long as the module's `go` line says 1.27 or later
choices.why: The `go` line allows the method to exist; it does not make it satisfy anything. The capture ran under 1.27.1.

choices.text: No: a method with type parameters satisfies no interface method
choices.why: Right. An interface asks for one signature a value has now; a generic method is a family that exists only per call.

choices.text: Only after an explicit conversion to the interface type
choices.why: A conversion to an interface needs the same method set; it cannot add what the assignment lacked.

prompt: A method cannot narrow `Stack[T any]`'s constraint, so a search using `==` becomes a function: `func Contains[T ___](s *Stack[T], v T) bool`.
hint: The predeclared constraint for types that `==` works on.
